summary_html: Agency decides to **remove a child immediately** due to **imminent danger** prior to a court order. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) requires later **court findings** on reasonable efforts; constitutional limits (due process; search/seizure) apply.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — monitors safety & removal decision quality

key_cases.case_name: Roska ex rel. Roska v. Peterson
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers who entered a family's home and removed a child without a warrant, court order, or exigent circumstances violated the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, rejecting the argument that the 'special needs' doctrine excuses the warrant requirement for child welfare removals.
key_cases.relevance: This is the governing Tenth Circuit rule for the emergency removal decision: no warrant and no exigency means an unconstitutional seizure.
key_cases.quote: We find no special need that renders the warrant requirement impracticable when social workers enter a home to remove a child, absent exigent circumstances

key_cases.case_name: Lowther v. Children, Youth & Families Department
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed qualified immunity for an investigator and county defendants on a warrantless-entry claim, holding that under circuit precedent a reasonable official could believe reasonable suspicion of past abuse justified warrantless entry, so the law was not clearly established to the contrary.
key_cases.relevance: Officials deciding whether to enter and remove may rely on reasonable suspicion of past abuse without clearly violating the Fourth Amendment in this circuit.
key_cases.quote: a reasonable investigator or officer could reasonably believe warrantless entry was justified by reasonable suspicion of past abuse

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: In a case beginning with an anonymous hotline call, the court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to the child welfare specialist and the officer who directed a six-year-old's seizure and transport from school for questioning, while reversing as to the officer who merely transported the child and as to the Fourteenth Amendment familial association claim.
key_cases.relevance: The decision to take a child into custody must be supported by warrant, probable cause, or reasonable suspicion depending on the circumstances.
key_cases.quote: The district court correctly determined that two of the three defendants were not entitled to qualified immunity on the Fourth Amendment unlawful seizure claim

key_cases.holding: The court held the father's challenge to the temporary custody order moot because later adjudication and disposition orders superseded it, but retained the appeal under the public-importance exception and upheld K.S.A. 38-2243(f)(3) — the temporary custody standard — against vagueness and overbreadth attack.
key_cases.relevance: The court upheld the probable-cause threshold that Kansas uses to keep a child in temporary custody pending the CINC hearing.
key_cases.quote: K.S.A. 2011 Supp. 38-2243(f)(3) is neither unconstitutionally vague nor over-broad

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that an unwed father was entitled as a matter of due process to a hearing on his fitness before his children could be taken from him, and that Illinois' presumption of unfitness applied only to unwed fathers denied him equal protection.
key_cases.relevance: Even in an emergency framework, the Constitution requires an individualized fitness determination before the separation is made permanent.
key_cases.quote: as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: A later finding is allowed only if a delay is requested by law enforcement, a county or district attorney, the court, or health or mental health professionals, or exceptional circumstances are documented in the case file (DCF PPM 2511 C.). An allowable late finding requires the Child Protection Specialist to enter "Allowable Delay" on the PPS 2011 Case Findings Section IV on or before the case finding due date; if the finding is late for a reason not allowable under PPM 2511 C., the specialist shall document with the finding: "The case finding is delayed due to a non-allowable reason per policy." (DCF PPM 2531 E.)
